title: How Much Does a Website Cost Per Month for a Small Business?
targetKeyword: how much does a website cost per month for a small business
excerpt: A small business website costs $30 to $700+ a month depending on who builds and runs it. Here is what each monthly cost covers and how to choose.

seo.metaTitle: How Much Does a Website Cost Per Month? (Small Business)
seo.metaDescription: A small business website costs $30 to $700+ a month. See what hosting, maintenance, updates and SEO really cost, with 3-year totals for each option.
keywords: how much does a website cost per month for a small business

body:
How much does a website cost per month for a small business? In most cases, between $30 and $700 a month. A DIY website builder costs $30 to $60 a month if you do the work yourself. A site built by an agency usually costs $50 to $300 a month to host and maintain after you have paid for the build. A done-for-you website subscription, where one company designs, builds and runs everything, typically costs $100 to $700 or more a month with nothing to pay upfront.

The right number depends less on the website itself and more on who does the work: you, a freelancer you call when something breaks, or a team that looks after it every month. This guide breaks down every monthly cost, shows real three-year totals, and helps you decide what your business should actually pay.

The quick answer: monthly website costs by option

OptionTypical monthly costUpfront costWhat you get
DIY website builder$30–$60$0Template, hosting and tools. You design, write and update it yourself.
One-off build + care plan$50–$300$2,000–$15,000Custom site, then hosting, backups and some updates. Bigger changes billed extra.
Website subscription$100–$700+Usually $0Design, build, hosting, security, updates and often SEO in one fee.

What you are actually paying for each month

Whichever route you choose, the same building blocks sit underneath every small business website. Knowing what each costs on its own helps you spot a fair price and avoid paying twice.

  • Domain name: about $10 to $20 a year for a .com or .co.uk, so roughly $1 to $2 a month. It should always be registered in your name.
  • Hosting: $5 to $50 a month. Cheap shared hosting is fine for a brochure site; booking systems and online stores need faster, more reliable hosting.
  • SSL certificate: often free with good hosting. Without it, browsers warn visitors your site is not secure.
  • Business email: about $6 to $7 per mailbox a month with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
  • Maintenance and security: $50 to $200 a month for backups, software updates, uptime and security monitoring. Skipping this is how small business sites get hacked or quietly break.
  • Content updates: agencies and freelancers usually charge $50 to $150 an hour for changes such as new prices, photos or pages.
  • SEO and Google Business Profile: ongoing local SEO is commonly a separate retainer of $300 to $1,500 a month.
  • Apps and add-ons: booking tools, forms, chat widgets and review apps each add $10 to $100 a month.

Add those up and a typical small business that buys everything separately spends $100 to $400 a month after launch, before any SEO, even though the website itself was already paid for.

Option 1: a DIY website builder ($30–$60 a month)

Builders such as Wix, Squarespace and Shopify are the cheapest way to get online. The monthly plan covers hosting, security and the editing tools, and many include a free domain for the first year.

The real cost is your time. Designing the site, writing the copy, setting up SEO and keeping it up to date can take 20 to 40 hours to start, and a few hours every month after. A DIY site makes sense if you have more time than budget, you need a simple site, and you are comfortable with design and writing. It struggles when you need custom booking, quote calculators or strong local search rankings in a competitive area.

Option 2: a one-off build plus a care plan ($50–$300 a month)

This is the traditional agency model. You pay $2,000 to $15,000 upfront for a custom website, then a smaller monthly fee for hosting and maintenance. The site is usually yours outright once it is paid for.

The catch is everything outside the care plan. Text changes, new pages, fixes after a plugin update and SEO are often billed separately. Many small businesses end up with a website that looked great at launch and is out of date two years later, because every change came with an invoice. Most one-off sites also need a redesign every three to five years, which means paying the upfront cost again.

Option 3: a website subscription ($100–$700+ a month)

With a website subscription, sometimes called website as a service, one company designs and builds your site and then runs it for a single monthly fee. Hosting, security, backups and content updates are included, and higher plans add booking systems, SEO and reporting. There is usually no upfront cost.

The trade-off is that you keep paying for as long as you use the service, and you need to check the contract carefully: how long is the minimum term, and what happens to the website if you cancel? We compare both models in detail in web design subscription vs one-time payment.

Real example: an 8-page website for a local plumber

Here is what the same website might cost over three years with each approach. Figures are typical, not quotes.

 DIY builderOne-off build + careSubscription
Upfront$0$6,000$0
Monthly$45 + $15 apps$100 care + ~$50 changes$199
Year 1 total$720$7,800$2,388
3-year total$2,160 + your time$11,400$7,164
Who keeps it updatedYouYou request and pay per changeIncluded

The DIY site is the cheapest in money but not in time. The one-off build costs the most in the first year. The subscription spreads the cost and includes the updates, but over five years or more a one-off site with light maintenance can work out cheaper, as long as you do not need many changes or a redesign.

Hidden monthly costs to watch for

  • Booking and marketplace fees: some booking apps charge per appointment or take a commission on new clients.
  • Payment and app fees: online stores pay transaction fees on top of the plan, plus monthly fees for each app.
  • Renewal price jumps: introductory hosting and builder prices often double on renewal.
  • Exit costs: some providers charge to transfer your site or keep the design when you leave. Ask before you sign.
  • Lost enquiries: a slow or outdated website costs you customers every month, which rarely shows up on an invoice.

How to decide what your business should pay

Start with what the website needs to do. If it is an online business card that rarely changes, a DIY builder or a simple one-off site is enough. If it needs to win enquiries every week, take bookings and rank in local search, budget for ongoing care, because a website like that is never really finished.

A useful rule of thumb: your website should pay for itself with one or two new customers a month. For a plumber, cleaner or clinic where a customer is worth hundreds of dollars, a $200 to $400 monthly plan that brings in even a few extra jobs is easy to justify. For a hobby business, it is not.

Ask any provider these questions: What exactly is included each month? How many changes can I request? Is there a minimum contract? Who owns the domain, content and design? What happens if I cancel?

What about the UK?

UK prices follow the same pattern: roughly £25 to £50 a month for a DIY builder, £2,000 to £10,000 upfront for an agency build, and £75 to £500 a month for a pay monthly website. See our guide prices for pay monthly websites for UK small businesses.

What a website costs per month with Velaris

Our plans start at $199 a month for a custom website up to 5 pages with hosting, security, a business email and 10 content updates a month. Growth at $399 adds online booking, unlimited updates, on-page SEO and Google Business Profile management. Scale, from $699, adds custom software and AI. There is no setup fee and you can cancel with 30 days' notice.

Compare everything side by side on our small business web design packages page, or see how our web design subscription works.

Frequently asked questions

What is a reasonable monthly cost for a small business website?

For a site you run yourself, $30 to $60. For a professionally built and maintained site, $100 to $400 is typical, and $400 to $700 or more when it includes SEO, booking systems or custom software.

How much is website maintenance per month?

Usually $50 to $200 a month for hosting, backups, security and small updates. Content changes beyond that are often billed hourly.

Is it cheaper to build a website once or pay monthly?

Paying once is often cheaper over five years or more if you rarely change the site. Paying monthly is cheaper in the first few years and includes updates and support, which matters if your website needs to keep winning customers.

title: Web Design Subscription vs One-Time Payment: Which Is Better?
targetKeyword: web design subscription vs one time payment
excerpt: Should you pay monthly for a website or buy it outright? An honest comparison of costs over 1, 3 and 5 years, ownership, and which suits your business.

seo.metaTitle: Web Design Subscription vs One-Time Payment (Honest Guide)
seo.metaDescription: Web design subscription vs one-time payment: costs over 1, 3 and 5 years, who owns the site, pros and cons, and the questions to ask before you sign.
keywords: web design subscription vs one time payment
pay monthly website vs one off
is a website subscription worth it

body:
Choosing between a web design subscription vs a one-time payment comes down to three things: how much cash you want to spend upfront, how often your website needs to change, and how much you care about owning everything outright. Neither option is always better. A one-time payment usually wins on long-term cost if your site rarely changes. A subscription usually wins when your website needs regular updates, SEO and support to keep bringing in customers.

We sell monthly plans, so we will be upfront about where a one-off build is the smarter choice. Here is an honest comparison.

How each model works

One-time payment

You pay an agency or freelancer a fixed price, typically $2,000 to $15,000 for a small business site, and they design and build it. Once it is paid for, the website is usually yours. Hosting, maintenance and future changes are separate: you either manage them yourself or pay for a care plan and hourly updates.

Web design subscription

You pay a monthly fee, often $100 to $700, and the provider designs, builds, hosts and maintains the site for as long as you subscribe. Updates, security and support are included, and many plans add SEO, booking systems or reporting. There is usually little or no upfront cost. This model is also called website as a service or a pay monthly website.

Cost over 1, 3 and 5 years

Here is a realistic comparison for a small service business website. The one-off example assumes an $8,000 build and $100 a month for hosting and maintenance, with updates billed on top.

 One-off ($8,000 + $100/mo)Subscription $199/moSubscription $399/mo
Year 1$9,200$2,388$4,788
Year 3$11,600$7,164$14,364
Year 5$14,000$11,940$23,940
Extra changesBilled per change10 a month includedUnlimited
SEO, booking, reportingExtraSEO setup onlyIncluded

Two things stand out. First, the subscription is far cheaper in the early years, which matters if cash flow is tight. Second, a higher-tier subscription can cost more than a one-off build over five years, but it also includes work, such as ongoing SEO and booking systems, that would cost thousands extra with a one-off site. Compare like for like: the question is not just the price of the website, but the price of everything you need it to do.

Also remember that most one-off websites are redesigned every three to five years. If you count a second build in year four, the one-time payment often stops being the cheaper option.

Pros and cons of a one-time payment

  • Pro: you usually own the website outright once it is paid for.
  • Pro: lower total cost over many years if the site rarely changes.
  • Pro: you can move hosting or developers whenever you like.
  • Con: a large upfront cost, usually thousands of dollars.
  • Con: changes, fixes and SEO cost extra, so sites tend to go out of date.
  • Con: you are responsible for security, updates and backups, or for paying someone to handle them.

Pros and cons of a web design subscription

  • Pro: little or nothing upfront, with a predictable monthly cost.
  • Pro: updates, hosting, security and support are included, so the site keeps improving.
  • Pro: one team is responsible for results, not just for launch day.
  • Con: you pay for as long as you use the service.
  • Con: ownership terms vary: some providers keep the design if you leave.
  • Con: long minimum contracts with some providers make it hard to switch.

The ownership question

This is the most important thing to check with any subscription. At minimum, your domain name should be registered in your name, and your logo, content and customer data should always belong to you. What varies is the website design and code. Some providers let you buy the site out or transfer it when you leave; others keep it, and you start again elsewhere.

Neither is wrong, but you should know before you sign. At Velaris, your domain is registered in your name, your content and data are yours, and if you cancel we send you all your website files to host and manage yourself or with another provider. Plans are month-to-month with 30 days' notice.

Which should you choose?

Choose a one-time payment if

  • You have the budget upfront and want to own everything outright.
  • Your website is mostly informational and rarely changes.
  • You have someone in-house, or a developer you trust, to maintain it.

Choose a subscription if

  • You would rather keep cash for marketing, staff or equipment.
  • Your website needs to win enquiries every week and change as your business grows.
  • You want booking, SEO and updates handled without managing several suppliers.
  • You want a professional site now rather than saving for one.

Questions to ask before you sign

  1. What is included each month, and how many changes can I request?
  2. Is there a setup fee or a minimum contract term?
  3. Who owns the domain, content, design and code?
  4. What happens to the website if I cancel? Can I buy it out or transfer it?
  5. How quickly do you make changes, and how do I request them?
  6. What happens to the price after the first year?

The bottom line

If you want the lowest cost over many years and your site rarely changes, pay once. If you want no upfront cost and a website that is kept fast, secure and improving every month, a subscription is usually the better fit, as long as the ownership and cancellation terms are clear.

title: How to Rank on Google Maps and Get Into the Local 3-Pack
targetKeyword: how to rank on google maps
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to ranking higher on Google Maps: how the local 3-pack works, what to fix on your Business Profile, reviews, your website and citations.

seo.metaTitle: How to Rank on Google Maps (Local 3-Pack Guide)
seo.metaDescription: How to rank on Google Maps and win a spot in the local 3-pack: Business Profile setup, categories, reviews, your website and citations, step by step.
keywords: how to rank on google maps
how to rank on google map pack
how to rank higher on google maps

body:
How to rank on Google Maps comes down to three things Google says it uses for every local search: relevance (how well your Business Profile matches what someone searched), distance (how close you are to the searcher or the area they named) and prominence (how well known and trusted your business is, online and off). You cannot move your premises, so ranking higher means doing everything you can to be the most relevant and the most prominent option nearby.

This guide walks through the exact steps, in the order that usually makes the biggest difference for small service businesses such as plumbers, cleaners, salons, clinics and contractors.

What is the Google local 3-pack?

When someone searches for a local service, such as “emergency plumber near me” or “nail salon in Leeds”, Google usually shows a map with three businesses underneath it before the normal results. That block is the local 3-pack, or map pack. It gets a large share of the clicks and calls for local searches, because it shows reviews, opening hours, a call button and directions in one place.

The same signals decide where you appear inside Google Maps itself, so improving your map pack ranking also helps you rank higher on Google Maps.

Step 1: claim, verify and complete your Business Profile

Your Google Business Profile is the listing that appears on Maps. If you have not claimed it, search for your business on Google Maps, select “Own this business?” and follow the steps. Google may ask you to verify by video, phone, text, email or postcard. Until the profile is verified, it will not rank properly.

Then fill in every field. Incomplete profiles lose to complete ones. That means your exact business name, phone number, website, opening hours (including holiday hours), service areas, a description and attributes such as wheelchair access or online appointments.

  • Business name: use your real-world name only. Adding keywords like “Best Plumber London” breaks Google's guidelines and can get your profile suspended.
  • Address or service area: show your address if customers visit you. If you travel to customers, hide the address and set the towns or postcodes you serve.
  • Hours: keep them accurate. Google tends to favour businesses that are open at the time of the search.

Step 2: choose the right categories

Your primary category is one of the strongest relevance signals you control. Pick the one that best describes your core service, such as “Plumber”, “House cleaning service” or “Physiotherapist”, not a broad one like “Contractor”. Then add secondary categories for other things you genuinely do.

A quick way to choose: search for your main service in your town and look at the categories the top three businesses use. If they all use a more specific category than you, switch.

Step 3: add your services, products and photos

List every service you offer in the Services section, with a short description and price where it makes sense. This helps you show up for more specific searches, such as “boiler repair” rather than just “plumber”.

Upload real photos regularly: your team, your premises, your vehicles and before-and-after shots of your work. Profiles with fresh, genuine photos look more trustworthy and get more engagement, which supports prominence.

Step 4: build a steady flow of reviews

Reviews are one of the biggest prominence signals and the main reason people choose one business in the map pack over another. What matters is the number of reviews, how recent they are, the star rating and whether you reply.

  • Ask every customer, not just the ones you think are happy, ideally by text or email straight after the job, with a direct link to your review form.
  • Aim for a steady stream every month rather than a burst once a year.
  • Reply to every review, good and bad, politely and within a few days.
  • Never buy reviews or offer rewards for them. It breaks Google's policies and can lead to reviews being removed or the profile being restricted.

We cover simple ways to automate this in how to get more Google reviews without begging.

Step 5: make your website back up your profile

Google looks at the website linked from your profile to understand what you do and where. A strong local website is often what separates the businesses in the 3-pack from the ones just below it.

  • Put your business name, address or service area and phone number on every page, written the same way as on your profile.
  • Create a page for each main service, and service-area pages for the main towns you cover, with genuinely useful local detail rather than copies with the town name swapped.
  • Add LocalBusiness structured data so search engines can read your details reliably.
  • Make sure the site is fast and works well on phones, because most local searches happen on mobile.

Step 6: get consistent citations and local links

Citations are mentions of your business name, address and phone number on other sites: directories such as Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yelp, Yell in the UK and industry directories. Consistent details across them help Google trust that your information is correct. Inconsistent or duplicate listings do the opposite.

Links from local websites, such as suppliers, local news, sponsorships, community groups and trade associations, are strong prominence signals and harder for competitors to copy.

Step 7: keep the profile active

Profiles that are updated regularly tend to perform better than ones left alone. Post updates and offers, add new photos, update services and keep hours current. Check your profile's performance report every month to see searches, calls and direction requests.

How long does it take to rank on Google Maps?

Fixes to categories and profile details can show results within a few weeks. Building reviews, citations and local links takes longer, typically three to six months to move from page two of Maps into the 3-pack in a competitive area. In a small town with few competitors, it can be much faster.

Common mistakes that hold businesses back

  • Keyword-stuffed business names, which risk suspension.
  • Using a virtual office or PO box as an address, which breaks Google's guidelines.
  • Duplicate listings for the same business.
  • Different phone numbers or addresses on the website and directories.
  • Ignoring reviews or replying with copy-and-paste messages.
  • Setting service areas far wider than you really cover.

If your business is not appearing at all, start with why your business is not showing on Google Maps, which covers verification, suspensions and other causes.

Want us to handle it?

Our Google Business Profile management covers setup, optimisation, posts and review requests every month, and our local SEO services for small businesses build the service-area pages and citations that move you into the map pack. Both are included in our Growth plan. See plans and pricing.

Frequently asked questions

How do I get my business in the Google 3-pack?

Verify and complete your Business Profile, choose the most specific primary category, collect reviews steadily, and make sure your website and directory listings show the same name, address and phone number. Distance still matters, so you are most likely to appear for searches near your location or service area.

Can I pay to rank higher on Google Maps?

Not in the organic results. Google Local Services Ads and Maps ads appear above or alongside the 3-pack and are marked as sponsored, but they do not change your organic ranking.

Does adding keywords to my business name help?

It can appear to help briefly, but it breaks Google's guidelines and risks suspension, and competitors can report it. Use your real business name.

title: Why Is My Business Not Showing on Google Maps? 10 Causes and Fixes
targetKeyword: why is my business not showing on google maps
excerpt: Business not showing on Google Maps, even after verification? Here are the 10 most common causes, how to tell which one applies, and how to fix each.

seo.metaTitle: Why Is My Business Not Showing on Google Maps? (Fixes)
seo.metaDescription: Business not showing on Google Maps, even after verification? The 10 most common causes, how to check which one applies, and how to fix each one.
keywords: why is my business not showing on google maps
why is my business not showing up on google maps after verification
why is my business profile not showing on google

body:
If you are asking why is my business not showing on Google Maps, the answer is usually one of a handful of causes: the profile is not verified yet, it has been suspended, it is too new, you are searching from too far away, or Google does not see it as relevant or prominent enough for that search. The good news is that most of these can be diagnosed in a few minutes and fixed.

Start by working out whether your business is missing completely or just not ranking. Search Google Maps for your exact business name and town. If it appears, the profile exists and the problem is ranking. If it does not appear at all, the problem is the profile itself.

1. Your profile is not verified yet

Unverified profiles generally do not appear in Maps results. Sign in to your Google Business Profile and look for a prompt to verify. Google may offer video verification, a phone call or text, email, or a postcard, depending on your business. Video verification usually means recording your signage, premises or equipment and proof that you manage the business.

Fix: complete verification and make sure the details you submitted match what Google can see, such as signage and your website.

2. Verification is done, but the profile is still under review

A common question is why a business is not showing up on Google Maps after verification. After verifying, or after editing important details such as your name, address or category, Google can take days or sometimes a few weeks to review and publish the changes.

Fix: wait at least a week before making further changes, because repeated edits can restart the review. If it is still not visible after a few weeks, contact Google Business Profile support from the help menu in your profile.

3. Your profile has been suspended

If your profile disappeared suddenly, or shows a warning when you sign in, it may be suspended. Common reasons include keyword-stuffed business names, using a virtual office or PO box as an address, listing a service area much wider than you cover, or several profiles for the same business.

Fix: correct whatever breaks Google's guidelines, then submit a reinstatement request from your profile with evidence, such as a business licence, a utility bill and photos of your signage. Do not create a new profile to replace a suspended one; it usually makes things worse.

4. You are a service-area business searching by address

If you hide your address because you travel to customers, Google shows your business for searches in your service area but will not place a pin at your home. That is normal. It can feel like you are missing when you look for yourself on the map.

Fix: search for your service plus a town you cover, such as “carpet cleaning Bristol”, rather than looking for a pin, and check your service areas are set correctly.

5. You are searching from too far away

Distance is one of the three things Google uses to rank local results. A business ranking first on your phone at your premises may not appear at all for someone a few miles away. Results also change with your location, search history and the device you use.

Fix: test from different locations or ask customers in your area to search. To appear across a wider area, you need stronger relevance and prominence: more reviews, better categories, service-area pages on your website and local links.

6. Your primary category is wrong

If your primary category does not match what people search for, Google will not show you for those searches, even with a perfect profile. A plumber listed only as “Contractor” will struggle to rank for “plumber”.

Fix: choose the most specific category for your main service, then add secondary categories for other genuine services.

7. The profile is new or incomplete

New profiles with no reviews, no photos and missing details struggle against established competitors. Google has little evidence that your business is real, active and trusted.

Fix: fill in every field, add services, upload real photos, and start collecting reviews from recent customers. Our guide on how to rank on Google Maps covers each step in order.

8. There are duplicate listings

Two profiles for the same business, often from an old address or a listing created by someone else, split your reviews and confuse Google. Sometimes the duplicate is the one that shows, with your old details.

Fix: search for variations of your name and old addresses or phone numbers. Request ownership of any duplicate, then ask Google to merge or remove it.

9. Your details do not match across the web

If your website, Facebook page and directories show a different name, address or phone number from your profile, Google is less confident your information is correct, which weakens your ranking.

Fix: use exactly the same business name, address and phone number on your website and every listing, including Bing Places, Apple Business Connect and Yelp, plus Yell in the UK.

10. A filter is hiding you

Google filters out businesses that look too similar to another nearby result, such as two businesses in the same category at the same address, or a practitioner and their practice. Only one usually shows.

Fix: make sure each profile has a distinct name, category and phone number, and that it represents a genuinely separate business. Where they are not separate, a single profile is often the better option.

Why is my business profile not showing on Google Search?

The same causes apply on Google Search. If your profile appears in Maps but not in the panel on the right of search results when someone searches your name, check that the name on the profile matches your website and signage, and give new edits time to process.

How long does it take to appear on Google Maps?

A verified profile usually appears within a few days to two weeks. Ranking well for service searches, rather than just your name, typically takes a few months of reviews, profile activity and website improvements, depending on competition.

Get it fixed for you

If you would rather not troubleshoot it yourself, our Google Business Profile management service handles verification, suspensions, duplicates and ongoing optimisation, and our local SEO services build the website pages and citations that help you rank. Both are included in our Growth plan; see plans and pricing.

Frequently asked questions

Why did my business disappear from Google Maps?

Sudden disappearances are usually caused by a suspension, a recent edit under review, or a duplicate listing taking over. Sign in to your profile to check for warnings first.

Why can I see my business but my customers cannot?

Results depend on location and search history. You see your business because you are close to it and search for it often. Customers further away may see competitors who are closer or more prominent.

Should I create a new profile if mine is not showing?

No. A second profile for the same business breaks Google's guidelines and can lead to suspension. Fix the existing profile or ask Google support for help.

title: Website as a Service: 5 Examples, Pricing and How It Works
excerpt: What website as a service (WaaS) means, five common models with typical pricing, what is usually included, and the questions to ask before you sign up.

seo.metaTitle: Website as a Service: Examples, Pricing & How It Works
seo.metaDescription: Website as a service explained: five real-world models with typical monthly pricing, what is included, pros and cons, and questions to ask any provider.

body:
Website as a service (often shortened to WaaS) means paying a monthly fee for a website that someone else designs, hosts and maintains, instead of buying it once and looking after it yourself. It works like any other subscription: you get a working website and ongoing support for as long as you pay, usually with little or no upfront cost.

The term covers quite different offers, from a $30 DIY builder to a $5,000-a-month design team. Below are five common website as a service examples, what each typically costs and who it suits.

How website as a service works

Most WaaS providers follow the same pattern. You choose a plan, they build the site (or give you the tools to build it), and the monthly fee covers hosting, security, software updates and some level of changes and support. Higher plans add things like SEO, booking systems, e-commerce or reporting. Contracts range from month-to-month to 12 or 24 months.

The appeal is predictability. Instead of a $5,000 to $15,000 bill on day one and surprise invoices later, you pay one known amount every month.

5 website as a service examples

ModelTypical priceWho does the workBest for
1. DIY website builder$15–$60/monthYouSimple sites, tight budgets, plenty of time
2. Template site with setup$50–$150/monthProvider sets up, you request small changesGetting online fast with minimal effort
3. Done-for-you small business subscription$150–$700/monthProvider designs, builds and runs itService businesses that need leads and updates
4. WordPress care plan$50–$300/monthProvider maintains a site you already ownBusinesses that have a site and want it looked after
5. Unlimited design and development$2,000–$6,000/monthA dedicated team works through a request queueFunded startups and agencies with constant changes

1. DIY website builders

Platforms like Wix, Squarespace and Shopify are technically website as a service: you rent the software, hosting and templates for a monthly fee. They are the cheapest option, but you do the design, writing, SEO and updates yourself.

2. Template sites with setup

Some providers take a ready-made template, add your logo, text and photos, and host it for a modest monthly fee. It is quick and affordable, but every client in your industry may end up with a similar-looking site, and customisation is limited.

3. Done-for-you subscriptions for small businesses

This is what most people mean by website as a service: a custom-designed website built and run by one team for a monthly fee, typically $150 to $700. Hosting, security, content updates and support are included, and higher plans add SEO, online booking, CRMs or AI tools. It suits service businesses such as trades, clinics, salons and cleaners that need a site that wins enquiries without managing it themselves. This is the model we use; see how our web design subscription works.

4. WordPress care plans

If you already own a website, a care plan covers hosting, backups, security, plugin updates and a set amount of changes each month. It is website maintenance as a service rather than a full WaaS, because the site itself was built separately.

5. Unlimited design and development subscriptions

At the top end, productised agencies offer a team that works through unlimited requests for a flat monthly fee, often several thousand dollars. It is excellent value for companies with a constant stream of design and development work, and far more than most small businesses need.

What is usually included

  • Website design and build, either custom or template-based
  • Hosting, SSL certificate, backups and security monitoring
  • Software and plugin updates
  • Content changes, either a set number per month or unlimited
  • Support by email, chat or WhatsApp
  • On some plans: SEO, Google Business Profile management, booking, e-commerce and reporting

Pros and cons of website as a service

  • Pro: little or no upfront cost, which protects cash flow.
  • Pro: the site is kept fast, secure and up to date without you managing it.
  • Pro: one predictable bill instead of several suppliers.
  • Con: you pay for as long as you use it, so it can cost more than a one-off build over many years.
  • Con: ownership of the design and code varies between providers.
  • Con: long minimum contracts with some providers make switching hard.

For a full cost comparison, read web design subscription vs one-time payment and how much a website costs per month.

Questions to ask a website as a service provider

  1. Is the design custom or a template?
  2. How many changes can I request each month, and how fast are they made?
  3. Is there a setup fee or a minimum contract?
  4. Who owns the domain, content, design and code?
  5. What happens to the website if I cancel?
  6. Are SEO, booking or other tools included, or extra?

Frequently asked questions

Is website as a service worth it?

For most small service businesses, yes, if the provider keeps the site updated and the contract is flexible. It is less worthwhile if your site rarely changes and you are happy to manage hosting and updates yourself.

Is Wix website as a service?

In a broad sense, yes: you pay monthly for the platform and hosting. But you do all the design and maintenance, whereas a done-for-you WaaS provider does that work for you.

Can I start a website as a service business?

title: How to Reduce No-Shows: 9 Proven Ways for Appointment Businesses
excerpt: Missed appointments cost service businesses real money. Here are 9 proven ways to reduce no-shows, from reminders and deposits to easier rescheduling.

seo.metaTitle: How to Reduce No-Shows: 9 Proven Ways (With Examples)
seo.metaDescription: How to reduce no-shows for clinics, salons and service businesses: reminders, deposits, easy rescheduling, waitlists and the booking setup that works.
keywords: how to reduce patient no shows

body:
If you run an appointment business, you already know how much no-shows cost: an empty chair, a wasted slot and staff paid to wait. The good news is that most no-shows are not people who never meant to come. They forgot, something came up and rescheduling felt like a hassle, or they did not feel committed. That means you can reduce no-shows a lot with the right reminders, policies and booking setup.

Here are nine proven ways to reduce no-shows, in roughly the order they make a difference.

First, measure your no-show rate

Your no-show rate is the number of missed appointments divided by the number booked, over a month. If 12 of 200 appointments were missed, your rate is 6%. Write it down before you change anything, so you can see which changes work. Track late cancellations separately: they hurt too, but need different fixes.

1. Send automatic reminders

Reminders are the single most effective fix, because forgetting is the most common reason people miss appointments. A simple sequence works well:

  • A confirmation straight after booking, with the date, time, address and what to bring.
  • A reminder 24 to 48 hours before, with a one-tap link to confirm or reschedule.
  • A short reminder 2 to 3 hours before for same-day appointments.

Text messages and WhatsApp are usually read faster than email, so use them where customers have agreed to be contacted that way.

2. Ask customers to confirm

A reminder people have to reply to ("Reply YES to confirm" or a confirm button) works better than one they can ignore. It creates a small commitment, and anyone who does not confirm can get a quick call or have their slot offered to someone else.

3. Make rescheduling easy

Many no-shows happen because cancelling felt awkward or required a phone call during working hours. Put a reschedule link in every reminder so customers can move their appointment in seconds. A rescheduled appointment is far better than an empty slot.

4. Take deposits for longer or high-value appointments

A deposit, even a small one, dramatically changes how committed people feel. It is common for salons with long colour appointments, detailers, tattoo studios and private clinics. Keep it proportionate, explain it clearly at booking and credit it against the final bill.

5. Have a clear, friendly cancellation policy

State how much notice you need (often 24 or 48 hours) and what happens if someone misses an appointment, such as losing the deposit or needing to prepay next time. Show it at booking and in the confirmation. Most customers respect a policy that is fair and clearly explained; apply it consistently but use judgement for genuine emergencies.

6. Keep a waitlist

A waitlist turns cancellations into bookings. When someone cancels or does not confirm, offer the slot automatically to people waiting for an earlier appointment. For busy clinics and salons this can recover a large share of lost time.

7. Shorten the gap between booking and appointment

Appointments booked weeks in advance are missed more often than ones booked for the next few days, because plans change and memory fades. Where you can, keep some short-notice availability and send an extra reminder for anything booked far ahead.

8. Let customers book online, any time

Online booking lets customers choose a time that genuinely suits them, rather than whatever was offered on a rushed phone call, and it captures their mobile number and email for reminders automatically. Booking systems built into your website also avoid marketplace fees and keep the customer relationship with you.

9. Follow up after a no-show

Send a friendly message after a missed appointment offering a new time. It recovers some of those customers, and the polite reminder that you noticed usually makes them more reliable next time. Track repeat no-shows and ask them to prepay or pay a deposit.

How to reduce patient no-shows in clinics

Clinics face extra challenges: longer booking lead times, anxious patients and appointments people put off. The same principles apply, with a few additions: send preparation instructions with reminders so patients feel ready, offer telehealth or a quick call when appropriate, and use recall messages to bring patients back for follow-ups at the right time. An AI receptionist for medical practices can also handle rescheduling out of hours.

The booking setup that reduces no-shows

The most reliable approach is to automate all of the above in one system: online booking, confirmations, reminders with confirm and reschedule links, deposits where needed, a waitlist and follow-ups. That is what we build for clinics, salons and spas and car detailers. Online booking with automated reminders is included in our Growth plan; see our booking systems for small business and pricing.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good no-show rate?

It varies by industry, but most appointment businesses aim to keep no-shows in the low single digits as a percentage. Track your own rate monthly and focus on improving it rather than comparing with others.

Do reminder messages really reduce no-shows?

Yes. Forgetting is the most common reason for missed appointments, so timely reminders with an easy way to confirm or reschedule are usually the biggest single improvement.

Is it OK to charge for no-shows?

Yes, as long as the policy is clear and agreed at booking. Many businesses take a deposit or charge a fee for missed appointments without enough notice.

title: How to Get More Google Reviews (Without Begging)
targetKeyword: how to get more google reviews
excerpt: A simple, policy-safe system to get more Google reviews: when to ask, what to say, how to make it one tap, and how to reply. Templates included.

seo.metaTitle: How to Get More Google Reviews (Templates Included)
seo.metaDescription: How to get more Google reviews without begging: when to ask, what to say, a one-tap review link, message templates and the rules Google enforces.
keywords: how to get more google reviews
how to ask for google reviews

body:
Knowing how to get more Google reviews is one of the most valuable things a local business can learn. Reviews influence where you appear on Google Maps, and they are often the deciding factor when a customer compares three businesses in the map pack. Yet most businesses only get a review when a customer happens to think of it.

You do not need to beg. You need a simple system: ask every customer at the right moment, make it take seconds, and reply to every review. Here is how to set it up, with templates you can copy.

Why Google reviews matter

  • Rankings: the number, recency and rating of your reviews are part of how Google judges your prominence in local search.
  • Clicks: businesses with more and better reviews get more calls, website visits and direction requests from the same position.
  • Trust: customers read reviews to decide whether you are reliable, and your replies show how you treat people.

Step 1: get your Google review link

Sign in to your Google Business Profile, choose "Ask for reviews" (or "Get more reviews"), and copy the short link. It opens the review box directly, so customers do not have to search for you. Save it somewhere your whole team can use it.

Step 2: ask at the right moment

Timing matters more than wording. Ask when the customer has just experienced the result: straight after a clean, when the car is handed back, at the end of a treatment, or the day a project is finished. A request sent within a few hours gets far more responses than one sent a week later.

Step 3: ask every customer, not just the happy ones

Google's policies prohibit "review gating": filtering customers so only happy ones are asked, or sending unhappy customers somewhere else first. Ask everyone in the same way. If you do great work, the vast majority of reviews will be positive, and a few honest mixed reviews make your rating more believable.

Also avoid offering anything in return for a review, such as discounts, entries into prize draws or freebies. Incentivised reviews break Google's policies and can be removed, along with any reviews posted by you, your staff or family.

Step 4: make it one tap

The fewer steps, the more reviews. Send the link by text or WhatsApp, where it opens straight on the phone, rather than asking people to search for you later. In person, a small card or sign with a QR code that opens your review link works well at reception or on invoices.

Step 5: automate the request

The reason most businesses get few reviews is that asking depends on someone remembering. Automate it: when a booking is marked complete or an invoice is paid, a review request goes out automatically, with one gentle reminder a few days later if they have not left one. This one change usually brings the biggest increase, because every customer is asked, every time.

Review request templates

Text or WhatsApp after the job

Hi [Name], thanks for choosing [Business] today. If you have a minute, a quick Google review would really help us: [link]. Thank you! [Your name]

Email after a project

Hi [Name], it was a pleasure working on [project]. If you have two minutes, we'd be grateful for an honest Google review about your experience: [link]. It helps other local customers find us. Thanks again, [Your name]

Gentle reminder

Hi [Name], just a quick reminder in case you missed it: here's the link to leave a Google review for [Business]: [link]. No worries if you're busy, and thanks again!

Step 6: reply to every review

Reply to every review within a few days. Thank positive reviewers by name and mention what they used, which reads naturally and reinforces what you do. For negative reviews, stay calm, apologise for the experience, offer to resolve it offline and keep it short. Future customers read your replies as closely as the reviews.

Step 7: show reviews on your website

Feature recent reviews on your homepage and service pages, near your calls to action. It builds trust at the moment people decide whether to contact you, and reminds visitors that you are active and well regarded.

How many reviews do you need?

There is no magic number. Look at the businesses in the top three for your main search in your area and aim to match or beat their count over time, while keeping a steady flow of new reviews every month. Recent reviews matter: ten reviews this year count for more with customers than fifty from five years ago.

Put your review requests on autopilot

Review requests are built into our Google Business Profile management on the Growth plan, alongside profile optimisation and directory listings, and work hand in hand with our local SEO services. For the bigger picture, read how to rank on Google Maps, or see plans and pricing.

Frequently asked questions

Can I ask customers for Google reviews?

Yes. Google encourages businesses to ask customers for reviews. What is not allowed is offering incentives, asking only happy customers, or writing reviews yourself.

Can I remove a bad Google review?

Only if it breaks Google's policies, such as spam, fake reviews, hate speech or a review about a different business. You can report it from your Business Profile. Otherwise, the best response is a calm, helpful reply.

Why did my Google reviews disappear?

Google's filters sometimes remove reviews that look suspicious, such as several reviews from the same location in a short time or reviews linked to incentives. Keep your requests natural and spread out over time.

body:
The best booking app for small business depends on what kind of business you run. A consultant booking video calls needs something very different from a nail salon managing six chairs or a cleaning company scheduling recurring visits across town. Picking the most popular app rather than the right one is how businesses end up paying for features they never use, or missing the one they need.

Below we compare eight widely used booking apps by the type of business they suit best, the questions to ask before choosing, and when a booking system built into your own website is the better option. We build custom booking systems, so we will be clear about when you do not need one.

Quick comparison

AppBest forStrengthsWatch out for
CalendlyConsultants, coaches, sales callsVery simple, connects to Google and Outlook calendars, video linksNot built for staff rotas, rooms or service menus
Acuity SchedulingTherapists, trainers, small studiosIntake forms, packages, payments, Squarespace integrationTakes time to set up well
Square AppointmentsSalons, barbers, spasBooking, payments and point of sale in oneCard processing fees on every payment
FreshaSalons and beauty businessesBeauty-focused features and a consumer marketplaceFees for marketplace clients and payments; check current pricing
BooksyBarbers and beauty professionalsPopular consumer app, client remindersSubscription plus extra fees for marketplace promotion
SetmoreVery small teams on a budgetEasy setup, free plan availableFewer advanced features
JobberCleaning, lawn care and tradesQuotes, scheduling, invoicing and job managementMore than you need if you only want bookings
Housecall ProHVAC, plumbing and home servicesDispatch, online booking, invoicing and reviewsPriced for growing teams rather than sole traders

Pricing changes often, so check each provider's current plans before you decide. Several offer free plans or free trials for one person.

Best booking app by type of business

Consultants, coaches and professional services

If you mostly book calls and meetings, Calendly is hard to beat for simplicity: share a link, people choose a time, and it lands in your calendar with a video link. Acuity Scheduling suits you better if you need intake questionnaires, packages or paid sessions.

Salons, barbers and spas

Beauty businesses need service menus, staff calendars, deposits and rebooking. Square Appointments works well if you also want card payments and a point of sale. Fresha and Booksy add a consumer marketplace that can bring new clients, but the fees for marketplace bookings and payments add up, and the client relationship partly lives on their platform. For a nail salon or small hair salon, the best choice is usually the one your clients already find easy, with deposits for long appointments.

Cleaning companies

Cleaners need recurring bookings, quotes that depend on home size and extras, and route-friendly scheduling. A field-service tool like Jobber covers quotes, recurring visits and invoicing. Simple appointment apps struggle with "every second Tuesday, 3 bedrooms, plus oven clean", which is why many cleaning companies add an instant quote calculator to their website. See our cleaning company websites.

Clinics and therapists

Clinics need reminders that cut no-shows, intake forms, recalls for follow-up appointments and careful handling of patient information. General apps can work for small practices; larger clinics usually need practice-management software or a booking system connected to it. Read how to reduce no-shows for the reminder setup that works.

Trades and home services

Plumbers, electricians and HVAC companies rarely book fixed slots weeks ahead; they need quote requests, emergency call-outs and dispatch. Housecall Pro and Jobber are built for this. For many smaller trades, a fast quote form and instant reply on the website matter more than a booking calendar. See contractor websites.

What to look for in any booking app

  • Automatic reminders by email and text, with an easy way to confirm or reschedule.
  • Deposits or card on file for long or high-value appointments.
  • Calendar sync with the calendar you already use, so you are never double-booked.
  • Booking from your website, not only from the app's own page or marketplace.
  • Fees you understand: subscription, per-staff charges, payment processing and marketplace commissions.
  • Your data: can you export your customer list if you switch?

Booking app or a custom booking system?

For most small businesses starting out, a good off-the-shelf app is the right answer. A custom booking system built into your website makes sense when:

  • you pay for several apps that do not talk to each other (booking, quotes, CRM, reviews);
  • marketplace commissions are eating into your margins;
  • your pricing or scheduling is too specific for standard apps, such as quotes by property size or recurring routes;
  • you want customers to book, pay deposits and get reminders entirely under your own brand.

That is what we build in our booking systems for small business, with online booking and automated reminders included in our Growth plan. See plans and pricing, or the systems we build for salons and spas and clinics.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best free booking app for a small business?

Calendly, Setmore and Square Appointments all offer free plans suited to one person or a very small team. They are a sensible way to start; upgrade when you need staff calendars, deposits or advanced reminders.

What is the best booking app for cleaning services?

A field-service tool such as Jobber is usually a better fit than a simple appointment app, because cleaning companies need quotes, recurring visits and invoicing. Add an instant quote calculator on your website to turn visitors into bookings.

Should my booking system be on my website?

Yes, ideally. Booking from your own website keeps customers on your brand, avoids marketplace fees and lets your website rank for searches like "book a cleaner near me".

title: AI Receptionist for Medical Offices: What It Costs and What It Can Do
targetKeyword: ai receptionist for medical office cost

seo.metaTitle: AI Receptionist for Medical Offices: Cost and What It Does
seo.metaDescription: How much an AI receptionist costs for a medical office, compared with front-desk staff and answering services, plus privacy, HIPAA basics and setup.
keywords: ai receptionist for medical office cost
ai receptionist for small business cost
best ai receptionist for medical practice
ai front desk for medical office

body:
An AI receptionist for a medical office typically costs anywhere from about $50 to over $700 a month, depending on whether you buy software and set it up yourself or have it designed, connected and managed for you. That is a fraction of the cost of extra front-desk staff, but price is only half the question. What matters for a practice is what the AI can safely handle, how it protects patient information and how well it fits your existing booking system.

This guide breaks down the costs, what an AI receptionist can and cannot do in a medical, dental or physio practice, and the privacy questions to ask before you choose one.

What an AI receptionist does in a medical practice

An AI receptionist answers patients on your website, and in some setups by phone or messaging, at any hour. In a typical practice it handles:

  • questions about opening hours, location, parking, services, prices and insurance accepted;
  • new appointment bookings, rescheduling and cancellations;
  • new-patient enquiries, collecting contact details and the reason for the visit;
  • preparation instructions, such as what to bring or how early to arrive;
  • handing anything clinical, urgent or unclear to your staff with the conversation attached.

What it should not do is give medical advice, triage symptoms or make clinical decisions. A well-set-up assistant answers only from information your practice approves and tells patients to contact emergency services when that is appropriate.

AI receptionist cost: the main options

OptionTypical costWhat you get
Self-serve AI chatbot software$50–$300/monthSoftware you configure, train and maintain yourself
AI phone receptionist software$100–$500+/monthAnswers calls; often priced by minutes or calls
Done-for-you AI receptionist$300–$1,000+/monthDesigned, trained on your practice, connected to your booking system and monitored for you
Human answering serviceOften $200–$800+/monthLive agents taking messages, usually billed per call or minute
Extra front-desk staff memberRoughly $35,000–$45,000+ a year in the US, before benefitsA person on site during working hours

These are typical market ranges rather than quotes. The cheapest software looks attractive, but the real cost includes the time to set it up properly, train it on your services, connect it to your calendar and keep its answers up to date.

What affects the price

  • Channels: a website assistant costs less than phone answering, which is usually priced by usage.
  • Integrations: connecting to your scheduling or practice-management system adds setup work but removes manual booking.
  • Volume: per-minute or per-conversation pricing grows with patient numbers.
  • Management: whether someone reviews conversations, updates answers and fixes gaps for you each month.

Is an AI receptionist worth it for a practice?

For most small and mid-sized practices, the value comes from three places. First, missed enquiries: patients who contact you in the evening or when the phones are busy often book with the next practice instead. Second, staff time: hours, directions and insurance questions take up a large share of front-desk time. Third, no-shows: easier rescheduling and reminders keep the diary full. If an assistant books even a handful of extra appointments a month, it usually covers its cost.

Patient privacy and HIPAA basics

In the US, any vendor that creates, receives or stores protected health information on your behalf generally needs a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with your practice under HIPAA. Before choosing an AI receptionist, ask:

  1. Will the assistant collect any protected health information, or only what booking requires?
  2. Will the vendor sign a BAA if it does?
  3. Where are conversations stored, for how long, and who can access them?
  4. Can clinical records stay in your practice software rather than the chat tool?

A sensible approach for many practices is to keep the assistant focused on booking and practical questions, collect only what scheduling needs, and keep clinical information in your existing systems. This is general information, not legal advice; check requirements with your compliance adviser. In the UK, the same principle applies under UK GDPR.

How to set up an AI receptionist

  1. List the 20 to 30 questions your front desk answers most often, with your approved answers.
  2. Decide what the assistant may do (answer, book, reschedule) and what it must hand to staff.
  3. Connect it to your calendar or scheduling system, or start with booking requests your team confirms.
  4. Test it with real questions, including tricky and urgent ones, before going live.
  5. Review conversations every month and update answers where patients get stuck.

It is included in our Scale plan from $699 a month, together with your website, hosting and integrations, with no setup fee. You can try the same technology with Ava, the assistant on our site. See our AI receptionist for medical practices, our AI receptionist for small business page, or pricing.

Frequently asked questions

How much does an AI receptionist cost per month?

Typically $50 to $300 a month for self-serve chatbot software, $100 to $500 or more for AI phone answering, and $300 to $1,000 or more for a done-for-you setup connected to your booking system and managed for you.

Can an AI receptionist replace front-desk staff?

Not entirely. It is best at repetitive questions, booking and out-of-hours enquiries, which frees your team to look after patients in the practice. Anything clinical or sensitive should still go to a person.

Is an AI receptionist HIPAA compliant?

Compliance depends on how it is set up and on the vendor's agreements, not on the technology alone. Limit what it collects, ask about BAAs and data storage, and check with your compliance adviser.
